description: I am a Chemical Engineering student from Pakistan, interested in environmental sustainability, pollution control, and innovative scientific solutions. I am participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge with my project, “earth detective.” I would love to collaborate with enthusiastic people who are interested in environmental science, data analysis, and graphic design , coding , web development
summary: Earth's environmental system is always changing. When change runs in a consistent direction (rising, falling, increasing, decreasing, thickening, thinning), measured variables reflect it as a trend. A variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The challenge is to build a tool that selects variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualizes how they change over time, and determines what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.
details:
What does it do?

Earth Science Trend Detective helps students and the public find out whether a change in NASA Earth data is real. The user picks a topic and a region. The tool fetches a time series, plots it, and reports what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

How does it work?

The user answers a few questions about topic, region and time period.

The tool matches them to NASA variables, such as MERRA-2 temperature or IMERG rainfall.

It pulls the regional series through NASA Earthdata.

It masks gaps and removes the seasonal cycle.

It fits a Sen slope and a linear regression, then runs the Mann-Kendall test and builds a confidence interval.

It shows the chart with a plain-language verdict and a warning if the record is too short.

Benefits:

Users don't need statistics or coding skills to test a trend.

Results are checked against published NASA trends, such as 3.4 mm per year of sea level rise since 1993.

It teaches that a weak trend can become significant with a longer record.

It labels data caveats, such as satellite changes in IMERG or model-based data in MERRA-2.

Intended impact:

More people can explore NASA Earth data and judge climate-related claims for themselves. It also helps teachers and students run real data investigations. [Add your own goal, such as a classroom pilot.]

Tools, languages, hardware and software

This is what I used to prepare the planning documents:

Claude for planning, research summaries and drafting.

Python (Matplotlib, SciPy, NumPy) for the diagrams and example charts.

JavaScript (docx library) for the Word file, and HTML/CSS for the slide deck.

NASA and USGS web pages for the facts.

The files were built in Claude's cloud workspace.

For the tool itself, the plan is:

Languages and libraries: Python with pandas, xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall and the earthaccess library.

Charts and interface: Plotly or Matplotlib, with Streamlit for the interface.

Data access: NASA Earthdata Login, Giovanni and GES DISC services.

Hardware: [your laptop or PC model, RAM, OS].

How is it creative?

It frames the user as a "data detective" who asks questions instead of reading raw numbers.

It gives a plain-language verdict next to the statistics.

It warns users when their time period is too short to trust.

It removes the seasonal cycle automatically, which hides trends in raw data.

It validates itself against real published NASA trends.

Two things to check before you submit

Only the planning, diagrams and slides exist so far. The tool's code is unbuilt, so describe the working parts as "planned" unless your team has built them.

Confirm that the team reviewed and tested the work, as your disclosure says.

I can also fit these answers to a word limit or turn them into a one-page handout.
